title: Evolution by Natural Selection

standard_text: Evidence for evolution (fossils, biogeography, comparative anatomy, genetics); variation; theories of evolution (Lamarck, Darwin, punctuated equilibrium); natural selection; artificial selection; speciation through geographic isolation; reproductive isolating mechanisms; evolution in present times (resistance to antibiotics and pesticides). (summary of the senior secondary Biology curriculum, SSS 3; WAEC and NECO syllabuses)
meta_desc: Free SSS 3 Biology worksheets (senior secondary curriculum, WAEC and NECO): evidence for evolution, natural selection, mechanisms of evolutionary change, speciation and artificial selection and resistance. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Individuals with useful variations survive and reproduce more.
key_sub: A species is a group that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
body_html:
How to think about it

Evidence for evolution comes from fossils, the distribution of species (biogeography), homologous structures (such as the pentadactyl limb) and similarities in DNA. Lamarck's theory (use and disuse, inheritance of acquired characteristics) was rejected. Darwin's theory of natural selection: there is variation; more young are born than can survive; those best suited to the environment survive and pass on their alleles.

Punctuated equilibrium proposes long periods of little change interrupted by quick change. New species form when a population is split by a geographic barrier and the groups change until they can no longer interbreed. Bacteria resistant to antibiotics (such as TB bacteria) and insects resistant to pesticides are evolution happening today.

Example

Why did Lamarck's idea not hold?

Can a giraffe pass on a stretched neck?

Answer: acquired characteristics are not inherited

Example

Antibiotic resistance spreads. Which process?

Survivors reproduce.

Answer: natural selection

Common mistakes

  • Thinking individuals evolve during their lives.
  • Thinking organisms change because they need to.
  • Thinking evolution means humans came from chimpanzees.

faq.q: Why must you finish a course of antibiotics?
faq.a: Otherwise the most resistant bacteria may survive and multiply.

faq.q: What is a reproductive isolating mechanism?
faq.a: Anything that stops two species from interbreeding, such as different breeding seasons or courtship behaviour.

items.q: Scientists compare a bat wing and a cat's front leg. They have the same bones in the same order. What does this suggest?
c: One species evolved from the other alive today.
The two species share a common ancestor.
The two species do the same job, so they are closely related.
items.e: Homologous structures point to common ancestry.

items.q: What kind of structures are these: the human tailbone?
items.e: Reduced and little or no use now.

the role of a species in its habitat

items.e: Two species cannot share exactly the same niche.

items.q: Why does biodiversity often increase during succession?
c: conditions become less hostile and more niches form

items.q: What does molecular evidence show about the relationships of species?
c: species with more similar DNA or protein sequences share a more recent common ancestor

items.q: What is an abiotic factor?
c: a non-living factor such as light or temperature

items.q: What is reproductive isolation?
c: changes that stop two populations interbreeding to give fertile offspring
items.e: It can be seasonal, mechanical or behavioural.

a sharp fall in population size that reduces genetic diversity
a mutation that blocks a gene
items.e: Cheetahs and Tasmanian devils show low diversity.

What does codominance mean?
c: both alleles are expressed in the heterozygote
the alleles are on different chromosomes
items.e: For example the AB blood group.
